title: Internal (endogenic) forces
competency: Distinguish endogenic and exogenic forces, and explain folding, faulting, earthquakes and volcanism and their landforms.

en.text: Geological processes are the natural forces that shape the earth. Endogenic (internal) forces start inside the earth and create relief by folding, faulting, earthquakes and volcanism. Exogenic (external) forces come from outside — running water, wind, ice, waves and gravity — and level the land by weathering, erosion and deposition. Geologists study them to understand earth history, find resources and predict disasters.

en.text: When rock layers are squeezed sideways they fold: upfolds are anticlines, downfolds are synclines. More pressure makes asymmetrical folds, over folds and over thrust folds. Young fold mountains formed in the latest (Alpine) mountain-building period: the Andes, Rockies, Alps, Himalayas and Atlas. Old fold mountains, such as the Appalachians, Urals and Scandinavian mountains, are lower and more weathered.

paras: Sideways compression bends rock layers.
Upfold: anticline. Downfold: syncline.

Old (first two periods): Scandinavian (Caledonian), Appalachians, Urals — lower and more weathered.

en.text: A fault is a crack in the crust made by tension or compression, along which rocks move up or down. Between two parallel faults, a sinking block forms a rift valley (graben), such as the East African Rift Valley, and a rising block forms a block mountain or horst, such as the Danakil (Afar) Horst. Rocks break in faulting but bend in folding.

en.text: An earthquake is sudden shaking when rocks slip along a fault, releasing stored energy as seismic waves. The focus is the underground starting point; the epicenter is directly above it. P waves arrive first, then S waves, then the slow but destructive surface waves. Seismographs record them. Most earthquakes occur in the Circum-Pacific belt (about 80 % of the energy) and the Mediterranean–Asian belt (about 15 %), and some along mid-ocean ridges and the East African Rift. Undersea quakes can cause tsunamis.

screens.after: The focus is the underground start; the epicenter is the surface point above it.

screens.title: What an earthquake is
paras: Rocks strain against each other along a fault and suddenly slip.
The energy spreads as seismic waves.
Most occur at the edges of plates.
Seismographs detect them; the Richter scale measures their magnitude on a logarithmic scale.

screens.title: Seismic waves
paras: Body waves travel through the earth: P (primary) push–pull waves, then S (secondary) side-to-side waves.
Surface waves (Love and Rayleigh) come last.
Surface waves are slowest but largest: they do most damage.

screens.title: Effects and occurrence
paras: Effects: ground cracks, landslides, mudflows, damage to buildings and dams, fires (San Francisco 1906, Tokyo 1923).
Tsunamis: up to 800 km/h in deep water and up to 30 m high at the coast.
Circum-Pacific belt (Ring of Fire): about 80 % of earthquake energy.
Mediterranean–Asian belt: about 15 %.
Also mid-ocean ridges and the East African Rift.
Shallow-focus quakes (< 60 km) release most of the energy.

en.text: Volcanism forces magma, gases and solids onto the surface through vents, which build cones, or fissures, which build lava plateaus. About 1,900 volcanoes are active, almost 90 % in the Pacific Ring of Fire; others lie on ocean ridges and in the East African Rift. Volcanoes are active (Erta Ale), dormant (Kilimanjaro) or extinct (Zuqualla). Shield volcanoes are broad (fluid basalt), strato volcanoes are steep and explosive, cinder cones are small cones of cinders. Craters and calderas are depressions; batholiths, sills and dykes are intrusions.

screens.after: An active volcano has erupted within about the last 500 years.

screens.title: Vents and fissures
paras: Magma underground; lava at the surface.
Vent: a pipe-like opening; lava builds a cone (a volcano).
Fissure: a long crack; lava spreads quietly and builds a plateau.

screens.title: Where and how active
paras: Most volcanoes are near plate boundaries: where plates diverge or converge.
About 1,900 active; almost 90 % in the Pacific Ring of Fire.
Others: ocean ridges, Indonesia, the Mediterranean, the East African Rift.
table: inactive now, erupted in history, may erupt

screens.title: Shapes and other landforms
paras: Shield: broad, gentle (≤ 7°), fluid basalt lava (Hawaii).
Strato: steep, alternating lava and ash layers, viscous lava, explosive; the most common.
Cinder cone: a small cone of cinders at the angle of repose.
Crater: a bowl at the top. Caldera: a large basin after the cone collapses into an empty magma chamber.
Intrusions: batholith (huge, deep), sill (horizontal), dyke (vertical).

screens.title: Key words
defs: Volcanism
The process by which magma, gases and solids are forced out onto the earth's surface.
Vent
A pipe-like opening through which magma reaches the surface; it builds a cone.
Fissure
A long narrow crack through which lava spreads quietly to build a plateau.
Caldera
A large basin formed when a volcano collapses into its emptied magma chamber.

notes.text: p.15: the Richter scale is not limited to 0–9 and measures magnitude, not "effect"; each step is about 10× amplitude and 32× energy. Figure 1.13 TNT equivalents are inconsistent.

p.13: the Australian Alps are old, not young (Alpine) fold mountains; "Calidonides" should be Caledonides. Figure 1.11 omits the Himalayas and labels the Drakensberg (not a fold mountain); "Tian Shen" should be Tian Shan.
p.14: "Afar Horst" is usually called the Danakil Horst. p.16: the S-wave sentence is garbled (the P–S time gap locates earthquakes).
p.18–19: energy by depth (>75 % + 12 % + 3 %) adds to 90 %; the first word of earthquake belts 1 and 2 is missing. p.21: craters and calderas are landforms, not types of volcano.
